      - Отмена в управляемых потоках
      - Свойство HttpContext.RequestAborted
      - Дедлайны и отмена в gRPC для .NET
      - Middleware таймаутов запросов в ASP.NET Core
  en:
    title: How do you design cancellation so that all work of an abandoned request stops across services?
    prompt: |
      An incoming request in ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) fans out to parallel calls to several downstream services, database
      queries and computation. The client closes the connection, or the time allotted to the request runs out.
      How do you design cancellation so that all the work this request started stops, and what must not or need not
      be stopped?
    hint: What does `Cancel` do to code that never received the token, and what does a cancellation signal become at a process boundary?
    answer: |
      1. **One token per request from two sources.** At the entry point take `HttpContext.RequestAborted` (in controllers
         and minimal APIs a `CancellationToken` parameter binds to it) and link it with the request's time budget:
         `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(requestAborted)` plus `CancelAfter(budget)`, or the request
         timeouts middleware (`AddRequestTimeouts`, added in .NET 8), which cancels `RequestAborted` itself.
         Dispose the linked source at the end of the request: it holds a registration on the parent token.
      2. **Pass the token explicitly and everywhere.** Every async method in the chain takes a `CancellationToken` and
         forwards it: `HttpClient.SendAsync`, EF Core `ToListAsync`, `Task.Delay`, `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync`, reads from a
         `Channel`. CPU-bound loops call `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` periodically. All fan-out branches get the same
         token; if a failure in one branch makes the others pointless, the branches get a child linked source that is
         cancelled on the first error.
      3. **Carry cancellation across the network.** A token does not travel over the wire. Cancelling an outgoing HTTP
         request aborts the connection or the HTTP/2 stream, and a downstream ASP.NET Core service sees its own
         `RequestAborted`. That covers only the abort; the budget has to travel as a deadline: gRPC sends it natively
         (the `grpc-timeout` header), and `EnableCallContextPropagation` in the gRPC client factory carries the deadline and
         cancellation of the current call into child calls; for HTTP you need your own header with the remaining budget,
         and each hop subtracts its own margin. A message already published to a queue cannot be cancelled: the consumer
         checks a deadline in the message, or the operation must be compensatable.
      4. **Decide what must not be cancelled.** Side effects past a point of no return (a committed transaction, a payment
         sent) are finished with `CancellationToken.None` or a separate short timeout, and operations are made idempotent so
         that a retry after an abort is safe. Work that must outlive the request goes to a queue or a background service,
         not to `Task.Run` with the request token.
      5. **Handle the outcome correctly.** `OperationCanceledException` caused by a client leaving is not an error: it is
         not logged as an error, not retried and not counted against the SLO. A client abort
         (`RequestAborted.IsCancellationRequested`) is told apart from an exhausted budget (a 504 or a domain error).
         Retry and hedging policies observe the same token and stop retrying once it is cancelled.
      6. **Verify.** Integration tests that abort the request and assert that downstream calls stop; tracing that shows
         cancelled spans; a check of proxies and load balancers, which may keep the backend connection open after the
         client leaves, so that `RequestAborted` fires late or not at all.
    explanation: |
      Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: `Cancel` only marks the token and runs the registered callbacks.
      Code that never received the token, or never checks it, runs to completion, so a single missed hand-off in the middle
      of the chain leaves the whole downstream request running. Hence the essence of the design: it is a contract in which
      every layer accepts and forwards the token, and every process boundary turns it into a protocol signal (a connection
      abort, a deadline) that becomes a token again on the other side.

      Linking with a budget matters as much as reacting to the abort: a client may wait longer than the work is worth,
      and without a shared deadline the lower services keep spending resources on a response nobody needs any more.

      Weak answers: `Task.WhenAny` with `Task.Delay` (it stops waiting but cancels nothing), only `HttpClient.Timeout`
      (100 seconds by default and only for a single call), a new `CancellationTokenSource` not linked to the request token,
      and cancelling everything without thinking about which side effects must not be interrupted halfway.
    linkTitles:
      - Cancellation in managed threads
      - HttpContext.RequestAborted property
      - Reliable gRPC services with deadlines and cancellation
      - Request timeouts middleware in ASP.NET Core

    title: Что такое пул потоков в .NET и когда лучше создать отдельный Thread?
    prompt: |
      Что такое управляемый пул потоков? Почему короткие задачи принято ставить в очередь пула
      (`Task.Run`, `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem`), а не создавать для каждой новый `Thread`?
      В каких случаях отдельный `Thread` всё же лучше?
    hint: Что станет с остальной работой в очереди пула, если один из его потоков навсегда занят бесконечным циклом?
    answer: |
      **Что это.** Пул потоков - это набор фоновых рабочих потоков, один на процесс, которым управляет среда выполнения.
      Код не создаёт потоки сам, а ставит в очередь рабочие элементы: `Task.Run`, `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem`,
      обратные вызовы таймеров, продолжения после `await`. Свободный поток пула берёт элемент из очереди, выполняет его
      и возвращается за следующим. Число потоков пул регулирует сам.

      **Зачем ставить короткую работу в пул.**
      - Создание и уничтожение потока стоит дорого: системный поток, память под стек, запуск и завершение.
        Для работы длиной в миллисекунды эти накладные расходы сравнимы с самой работой или больше её.
        Пул переиспользует уже созданные потоки.
      - Пул ограничивает число потоков, и тысяча коротких задач не превращается в тысячу потоков, которые
        конкурируют за ядра и память.
      - `Task` поверх пула даёт результат, передачу исключений, продолжения и отмену, чего у голого `Thread` нет.

      **Когда нужен отдельный `Thread`.**
      - Долгий или блокирующий цикл, который живёт всё время работы приложения: например, чтение из синхронного API
        устройства или очереди. Такой цикл навсегда занимает поток пула, а пул добавляет потоки сверх минимума
        постепенно, поэтому остальная работа начинает ждать в очереди.
      - Нужен поток переднего плана, который не даст процессу завершиться (потоки пула фоновые).
      - Нужен особый приоритет потока или однопоточный апартамент (STA) для COM: все потоки пула работают в MTA
        с приоритетом по умолчанию.
      - Нужна стабильная идентичность потока, то есть поток, выделенный под одну задачу.

      Для долгой синхронной работы в виде задачи есть `Task.Factory.StartNew` с `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`:
      стандартный планировщик тогда выполняет её не в потоке пула. Если же долгое ожидание связано с вводом-выводом,
      лучше вообще не держать поток и использовать асинхронный API с `await`.
    explanation: |
      Пул выгоден, потому что потоки в нём живут долго, а работа в них - коротко: дорогое создание потока
      оплачивается один раз и распределяется на множество рабочих элементов. Эта модель ломается, когда элемент
      не заканчивается. Число потоков пула ограничено, а сверх минимального значения новые потоки добавляются
      не мгновенно, поэтому несколько бесконечных или блокирующих циклов в пуле задерживают все остальные задачи,
      включая продолжения `async`-методов. Это прямой путь к голоданию пула потоков.

      Типичные ошибки - две крайности: создавать `new Thread` на каждый запрос или короткую операцию и, наоборот,
      запускать через `Task.Run` вечный цикл с блокирующими вызовами. Ещё одна ловушка - `LongRunning` с асинхронной
      лямбдой: выделенный поток выполняет её только до первого незавершённого `await`, а продолжение уходит в пул,
      так что опция теряет смысл. Поведение описано для .NET 10.

  en:
    title: What is the .NET thread pool and when is a dedicated Thread the better choice?
    prompt: |
      What is the managed thread pool? Why is short work usually queued to the pool
      (`Task.Run`, `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem`) instead of creating a new `Thread` for each item?
      When is a dedicated `Thread` still the better choice?
    hint: What happens to the rest of the work in the pool queue if one of its threads is busy forever with an endless loop?
    answer: |
      **What it is.** The thread pool is a set of background worker threads, one pool per process, managed by the runtime.
      Code does not create threads itself; it queues work items: `Task.Run`, `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem`,
      timer callbacks, continuations after `await`. A free pool thread takes an item from the queue, runs it
      and comes back for the next one. The pool adjusts the number of threads itself.

      **Why short work goes to the pool.**
      - Creating and destroying a thread is expensive: an operating system thread, memory for the stack, startup and teardown.
        For work that takes milliseconds this overhead is comparable to the work itself or larger.
        The pool reuses threads that already exist.
      - The pool limits the number of threads, so a thousand short work items do not turn into a thousand threads
        competing for cores and memory.
      - A `Task` on top of the pool gives a result, exception propagation, continuations and cancellation, which a bare `Thread` lacks.

      **When a dedicated `Thread` is needed.**
      - A long-running or blocking loop that lives for the whole lifetime of the application: for example, reading from a
        synchronous device or queue API. Such a loop holds a pool thread forever, and the pool adds threads above its minimum
        gradually, so the rest of the work starts waiting in the queue.
      - You need a foreground thread that keeps the process from exiting (pool threads are background threads).
      - You need a specific thread priority or a single-threaded apartment (STA) for COM: all pool threads run in the MTA
        at the default priority.
      - You need a stable thread identity, that is, a thread dedicated to one task.

      For long synchronous work expressed as a task there is `Task.Factory.StartNew` with `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`:
      the default scheduler then runs it outside the pool. If the long wait is about IO, it is better not to hold a thread
      at all and to use an asynchronous API with `await`.
    explanation: |
      The pool pays off because its threads live long while the work in them is short: the expensive thread creation
      is paid once and spread over many work items. That model breaks when an item never finishes. The number of pool
      threads is limited, and above the minimum new threads are not added instantly, so a few endless or blocking loops
      in the pool delay every other task, including continuations of `async` methods. That is a direct path to thread
      pool starvation.

      The typical mistakes are two extremes: creating `new Thread` for every request or short operation, or, the other way
      round, starting an endless loop with blocking calls through `Task.Run`. Another trap is `LongRunning` with an async
      lambda: the dedicated thread runs it only until the first incomplete `await`, and the continuation goes to the pool,
      so the option loses its point. The behaviour is described for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - The managed thread pool
      - TaskCreationOptions enum

  en:
    title: "A pricing cache returns corrupted data under load: should you accept one global lock before the release?"
    prompt: |
      A pricing service keeps its data in an in-memory cache: a singleton with a `Dictionary<string, PriceInfo>` that a
      background job refreshes every few minutes while requests read it. `PriceInfo` is a mutable class, and the job
      updates its fields in place. Under load a response rarely contains a price paired with the wrong currency, and once
      a request hung with a thread burning 100% of a core inside `Dictionary` code. The release is in two days. A
      developer proposes wrapping every cache access in one global `lock (Sync)` and shipping.

      What do you decide as the lead, and how does the team prevent this kind of bug from coming back?
    hint: Which state exactly is shared between threads and changed at the same time, and what does a single shared `lock` do to the hottest read path?
    answer: |
      1. **Assess the risk and decide on the release.** Wrong prices are a business incident, not a cosmetic one. Do not
         ship an untested "lock everything" patch in a hurry. Either the release moves, or it ships with a narrow fix of
         the confirmed cause (step 3) checked by a load test. A coarse lock is acceptable only as a temporary measure,
         if a load test shows acceptable throughput and no IO or other locks run under it. State the risk and the plan
         explicitly to the product owner.
      2. **Find the shared mutable state.** Make an inventory:
         - the `Dictionary` is written by the background job while requests read it. `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` supports
           concurrent readers only while nobody modifies it; a concurrent write can corrupt its internal structure,
           which explains the hang;
         - `PriceInfo` objects are changed field by field, so a reader sees the new price with the old currency. A `lock`
           inside the cache does not help here: references to `PriceInfo` escape to callers and are read outside the lock;
         - check-then-act sequences (`ContainsKey`, then the indexer) and lazy initialization.
      3. **Fix it by design, not by locking.** Make the values immutable (a `record` with `init` properties). The
         background job builds a whole new snapshot on the side (`ToFrozenDictionary()` in .NET 8 and later, including
         .NET 10, or a new `Dictionary` that is never modified after publishing) and publishes it by swapping one
         reference: `Interlocked.Exchange(ref _snapshot, next)` or `Volatile.Write`. A reader takes
         `var snapshot = Volatile.Read(ref _snapshot);` once and uses it for the whole request: it sees one consistent
         version without any lock. If per-key changes are needed between full refreshes, use
         `ConcurrentDictionary<string, PriceInfo>` and replace whole values instead of mutating their fields. There
         should be a single writer of the snapshot; with several, use `Interlocked.CompareExchange`.
      4. **Explain to the team why not a global lock.** It serializes the hot read path: every request queues for one
         lock, so throughput falls and latency grows exactly under load. Blocked threads hold thread pool threads. One lock
         taken from many places leads to deadlock as soon as someone calls IO, another lock or a callback under it. Any
         path that forgets it brings the race condition back, and it does not protect mutable objects that escaped at all.
      5. **Prove it and make it stick.** A stress test: many parallel readers and frequent refreshes for several minutes,
         checking an invariant (price and currency come from the same snapshot version), in CI or a nightly build. A code
         review rule: a singleton or static field with mutable state must have an explicit synchronization approach - an
         immutable snapshot with an atomic swap, a concurrent collection, or a documented lock. A blameless post-incident
         review and a short team session on the pattern.
    explanation: |
      The lead's job here is to tell suppressing a symptom from removing the cause, and to manage the release risk. A
      race condition comes from shared mutable state, and there are three ways to remove it: do not share, do not mutate,
      or synchronize. A global `lock` is the crudest form of the third: it hides the race at the cost of throughput and a
      new deadlock risk, and it still does not cover objects that leaked outside it.

      For a read-mostly cache the second way fits better. An immutable snapshot plus an atomic reference swap gives
      lock-free reads and consistency within one snapshot. Reference assignment in C# is atomic, and
      `Interlocked.Exchange` also adds a full memory barrier and returns the old value. The price is memory for two
      snapshots during a refresh and staleness up to the refresh interval, which a cache already accepts. Without a
      stress test and a review rule, the same bug comes back in the next singleton.
    linkTitles:
      - "Managed threading best practices"
      - "Interlocked.Exchange method"
      - "FrozenDictionary<TKey,TValue> class"
